source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Mateusz Pach; Shyamgopal Karthik; Quentin Bouniot; S. Belongie; Zeynep Akata

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature analysis to pretrained vision and vision-language model encoders, a new setting relative to the toy-model claim, and reports results about recovered feature interpretability. It does not test the original toy-network geometry.
record.gate_note: The study measures image-neuron monosemanticity and compares SAE latents with original model neurons. Human-study alignment results validate the proposed metric rather than directly test the claim versions. Steering outcomes are induced by intervention and are not evidence that the behavior or representation occurs naturally, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on pretrained vision encoders (CLIP, SigLIP, AIMv2, WebSSL). It reports that SAE latents are far more monosemantic than the original neurons, even at equal width. That bears on V4's claim that real models contain sparse features a dictionary can recover, here in vision encoders rather than LLMs. The steering and human-study results validate tools and are not tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: SAEs raise neuron-level monosemanticity in VLM vision encoders, mainly through sparsity and width, and Matryoshka SAEs do best. SAE neurons can also steer LLaVA, though high-MS neurons do not always steer precisely.
record.recipe_differences: Post-hoc BatchTopK and Matryoshka BatchTopK SAEs are trained on pretrained vision-model activations and evaluated with an image-similarity-based monosemanticity metric; the paper does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: MS varies with SAE width and sparsity. The authors report that stricter sparsity generally improves MS but reduces reconstruction quality; across all neurons, MS rises overall up to ε = 4 and then declines overall. Results also depend on the vision encoder used to compute image similarities, explored in the appendix.
record.problems: The evidence concerns vision encoder activations in VLMs rather than LLM activations, and the MS metric measures similarity of activating images rather than direct feature geometry. The paper reports that higher MS does not always yield precise steering effects and that Matryoshka SAE results trade reconstruction quality against interpretability. Several distributional comparisons are presented as plots or approximate textual summaries.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1a values at expansion factors ×2, ×8, and ×16, and many appendix tables of average, minimum, and maximum MS across layers and widths are omitted to stay within the row limit while retaining baseline comparisons, low/intermediate/high width examples, model comparisons, and sparsity conditions. Table 1b's CLIP result duplicates the CLIP result in Table 1a. Steering benchmarks and examples are excluded because the target behavior is deliberately induced by intervention, not a measure of naturally occurring representation.

untested.parts: LLM activations; feature spread across neurons in language models. Only vision encoders used in VLMs are tested.
Not tested: no toy models, sparsity-dependent transition or geometry.
Not tested: no test of importance-based capacity allocation.
Not tested: no alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
Completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested. Appendix G's low Jaccard overlap between latents bears only on redundancy.
Not tested: no 1-D versus multi-dimensional feature comparison.

missing.what: Mean MS at early layers is only slightly above No SAE, e.g. layer 11 BatchTopK ×1 0.03±0.06 vs 0.0135. The gain is concentrated in later layers.
With CLIP ViT-B as evaluator, mean MS gains are modest (No SAE about 0.48 vs SAE 0.52–0.63). SigLIP early layers show 0.50–0.54 vs 0.48. The authors say gains are less distinct.
missing.locator: Tables A3, A4, A6, A7; Figure A7

record.verdict_notes: Vision encoders are treated as a new setting for V4 (T3), not LLMs. Rows r1–r36 report max-neuron scores, so they overstate the typical gain. The mean-MS tables show the effect is much weaker at early layers and depends on the evaluator encoder. The original source (arXiv:2209.10652) is only cited.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-capacity sweep, near-orthogonal directions, or sparsity-dependent geometry transition are tested.
Does not test whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared neuron allocation or whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE-recovered features in vision encoders used in VLMs, not language-model activations or LLM-wide feature distribution.
Does not establish SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units; its uniqueness analysis does not test completeness or stability.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-L/14-336px
rows.operation_detail: Compared MS distributions across Matryoshka SAE widths.

conditions.value: all-neuron score distribution across expansion factors

rows.baseline: ε = 1 reference; exact plotted values not stated
rows.value: Scores increase overall up to ε = 4, then decrease overall; at very wide latents they can fall below ε = 1, while absolute counts of neurons at a given score still increase
rows.note: The authors distinguish the relative fraction of neurons at score levels from their absolute number.
rows.check: The comparison is between SAE widths, not against the No SAE baseline. Even the wide SAEs that fall below ε=1 stay above No SAE in Fig. 5a, so the decline qualifies the trend but does not remove the effect.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-L layers 11–last, SigLIP, AIMv2 and WebSSL last layers; BatchTopK and Matryoshka SAEs; DINOv2 evaluator
relationships.reason: SAE latents beat original neurons at every width: top MS 0.57–1.00 vs 0.01, and about 90% of ε=1 latents score higher than neurons (r1–r36, r41). Mean MS is also above baseline (r37–r39).
relationships.display_finding: Top monosemanticity scores were 0.57–1.00 for SAE latents against 0.01 for neurons, and about 90% of latents at ε=1 scored higher than neurons. Mean scores were also above baseline.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: CLIP ViT-L layers 11–last, SigLIP, AIMv2 and WebSSL last layers; BatchTopK and Matryoshka SAEs; DINOv2 evaluator
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms the reported maxima; Figure 5 and Table A2 independently support improved monosemanticity across neurons, including equal-width SAEs. Non-CLIP comparisons in Table 1b use Matryoshka SAEs.

relationships.condition: Looser sparsity (K=50), very wide SAEs, early layers, or the CLIP ViT-B evaluator
relationships.reason: Mean MS falls to 0.07 at K=50 (r40) and declines beyond ε=4 (r42). Per Tables A2–A4 (text), mean gains are small at early layers and with the CLIP ViT-B evaluator.
relationships.display_finding: Mean monosemanticity score fell to 0.07 at K=50 and declined for SAEs wider than ε=4, and mean gains were small at early layers and with the CLIP ViT-B evaluator.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Looser sparsity (K=50), very wide SAEs, early layers, or the CLIP ViT-B evaluator
source_check.reason: Recovery strength depends on these choices: Table A11 gives mean MS 0.07 ± 0.08 at K=50; Figure 5 describes declining score distributions beyond ×4; Tables A2–A4 show smaller mean gains in earlier layers and with the alternative evaluator. These qualify recovery strength rather than show absence.

relation.reason: Directly compares monosemanticity of recovered SAE features with original neurons, including aggregate comparisons.

tranche.reason: Tests sparse dictionary feature recovery in pretrained vision encoders, extending the setting of V4.

source_check.notes: All 25 checked rows accurately report selected maxima, but selection values should not stand alone as result rows under the supplied rules. Aggregate results substantiate the verdicts; the tested representations are vision encoders, and reported neuron-score standard deviations describe dispersion across neurons.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested pretrained vision encoders: CLIP, WebSSL, SigLIP, and AIMv2; reported SAE widths and layers
reader_labels.reason: SAE latents have higher MS than the original-neuron reference in the reported comparisons, including same-width SAE results (r1–r36, r41). This is evidence for recoverable, more monosemantic features in these vision encoders, not LLM activations.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Variation in sparsity and SAE width in the CLIP ViT-L experiments
reader_labels.reason: Mean MS is lower at K = 50 than at stricter sparsity settings, and the all-neuron score distribution declines beyond ε = 4; stricter sparsity also costs reconstruction quality (r37–r40, r42).
